newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Malaysia's Tenaga says still have investors faith.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's Tenaga says still have investors faith.

text.p: The downgrading of Malaysian Tenaga Nasional Berhad's credit rating was overdone as foreign investors continued to have faith in the company, a senior Tenaga official said on Wednesday.
"We are in contact with our lenders and creditors overseas," Rohailan Mohamed, Tenaga's Senior General Manager for Finance said. "We have told them what's happening. They have great faith in us."
He was speaking to reporters during the Asia-Pacific Petroleum Conference (APPEC) in Singapore.

Moody's Investor Service cuts its rating on Tenaga's unsecured debt to negative from stable following an August 3 peninsula-wide 12-15 hour power blackout and comments by Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that he did not rule out breaking Tenaga's monopoly on power distribution.
Tenaga's share price fell to a year's low of 8.75 Malaysian ringgit per share on Wednesday, before closing at 8.80 ringgit, down 20 cents from Tuesday.

The lower credit rating has raised fears foreign investors would find Tenaga's debt less attractive and so force the company to look more to the domestic market for funding. About 70-80 percent of Tenaga's debt is held in foreign hands.
The lower rating has prompted Tenaga's new chief executive Ahmad Tajuddin Ali to seek a meeting with Moody's, Malaysian newspapers have reported.
"Moody's gets a bit rattled," Rohailan said. "Probably if they don't do that they might be seen as not doing anything.
"But maybe they are overreacting because our cash flow is still the same. We are not affected. One blackout does not mean that we are going to lose a lot of revenue."
He said, "We have not actually sunk. We are still there. We will bounce back with our new chief executive. He has already promised some material and effective changes that we are looking forward to."
Tenaga reported a net profit of 1.243 billion ringgit in the year to the end of August 1995.
